title: The Constitution - rules for the rule-makers

---
order: 1
unit: government
title: The Constitution - rules for the rule-makers
node: AC9HC7K01 n1
summary: "Australia's Constitution is the written rulebook for the national government. It came into effect on 1 January 1901 and sets up Parliament, the Governor-General and the High Court, and it limits what Parliament can make laws about. Parliament cannot change it alone: any change has to be approved by the voters in a referendum. Students meet the idea first in a made-up club, then in the real thing."
language: maths
hook: "Parliament makes the laws for the whole country. But who makes the rules for Parliament?"
---
Something has to say what Parliament is, what it is allowed to do, and who can change those rules. In Australia, that is the **Constitution**.

You will start with a small version of the same idea: a club.

## Predict: the club's rules

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing to an answer first shows that rules apply to the people who make decisions too."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "The Maple Street Chess Club has a written rule: the committee can spend up to $200 without asking the members. The committee wants to spend $500. What should happen?"
  options: ["The committee asks the members to vote, because the rule limits what the committee can decide alone", "The committee goes ahead, because it runs the club", "The committee changes the rule at its next meeting, then spends the money", "Nothing, because rules are only suggestions"]
  actual: "The committee asks the members. The written rule limits the committee, so it cannot just go past it."
```

## Try: what goes in the club's rulebook?

```step
stage: run
insight: "Sorting shows that a constitution holds the big, lasting rules, and the committee makes everyday decisions inside them."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "Is each thing in the club's constitution, or something the committee decides week to week?"
  options: ["In the constitution", "Committee decides"]
  items:
    - ["That the club has a committee, and how it is chosen", "In the constitution", "A constitution sets up the club's decision-makers."]
    - ["What the committee may spend without asking the members", "In the constitution", "It limits the committee, so it has to be written above the committee."]
    - ["Which snacks to buy for Friday", "Committee decides", "This is an everyday decision made inside the rules."]
    - ["How many members must come for a vote to count", "In the constitution", "This is a lasting rule about how decisions are made."]
    - ["Which day to hold the next tournament", "Committee decides", "This is an everyday decision."]
    - ["How the rules themselves can be changed", "In the constitution", "A rulebook says how it can be changed."]
```

Was your guess right? Notice the pattern. A constitution sets up the decision-makers, says what they may and may not decide, and says how the rules themselves can be changed. Everyday decisions happen inside it.

### The real rulebook

```worked
\text{Who is it for?} :: The Constitution sets rules for the people who make the country's laws.
\text{What does it set up?} :: Parliament (makes laws), the Governor-General (formally appoints ministers and signs laws), the High Court (decides what the rules mean).
\text{What does it limit?} :: Parliament can only make laws about the subjects the Constitution lists, such as defence and the post.
\text{Who can change it?} :: Not Parliament alone. The voters decide, at a referendum.
```

Now: what is the Constitution's main job?

## Vary: more rules about the rule-makers

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Each task changes the case: what is written in the Constitution, what Parliament can do, and who has the final say."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "Is each thing set out in the Constitution, or decided by an ordinary law Parliament passes?"
      options: ["In the Constitution", "Ordinary law"]
      items:
        - ["That there is a Senate and a House of Representatives", "In the Constitution", "The Constitution sets up the two houses."]
        - ["The rules for getting a passport", "Ordinary law", "Parliament can pass and change this like any law."]
        - ["That there is a High Court", "In the Constitution", "The Constitution sets up the High Court."]
        - ["How much income tax is paid", "Ordinary law", "Parliament sets tax rates by passing laws."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Which of these could Parliament do just by passing an ordinary law?"
      options: ["Change the rules for getting a passport", "Get rid of the High Court", "Get rid of the Senate", "Give itself the power to make laws about anything it likes"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "The Constitution sets up the High Court, so getting rid of it would mean changing the Constitution.", "The Constitution sets up the Senate, so this too would need a referendum.", "The Constitution limits what Parliament can make laws about. Changing that would need a referendum."]
      explain: "Ordinary laws sit under the Constitution. Anything that changes the Constitution itself needs the voters."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "In the chess club and in Australia, who has the final say on changing the basic rules?"
      options: ["The members in the club, and the voters in Australia", "The committee in the club, and Parliament in Australia", "The president in the club, and the Prime Minister in Australia", "A court in both"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Think about why the rules exist. If the rule-makers could change them alone, the rules would not limit them.", "The president and Prime Minister are decision-makers too, so the same problem applies.", "A court explains what the rules mean. It does not change them."]
      explain: "The people the rules are meant to serve have the final say, not the people the rules limit."
```

Write it in your own book or document, not on this page. Your partner or teacher reads it.

## Typical: what is in the Constitution?

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "The Constitution is divided into parts. Matching each part to its job shows how the rulebook is organised."
check:
  type: match
  q: "Match each part of the Constitution to what it is about."
  pairs:
    - ["Chapter I: The Parliament", "The Senate, the House of Representatives and how laws are made"]
    - ["Chapter II: The Executive Government", "The Governor-General and the ministers who carry out the laws"]
    - ["Chapter III: The Judicature", "The High Court and other federal courts"]
    - ["Chapter VIII: Alteration of the Constitution", "How the Constitution can be changed"]
```

## Wider: did the referendum pass?

```step
stage: make
tier: wider
insight: "The double majority: a change needs a majority of all voters and a majority in at least four of the six states."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "A change to the Constitution needs a majority of all voters, and a majority of voters in at least four of the six states. Did each made-up proposal pass?"
  options: ["Passes", "Fails"]
  items:
    - ["Proposal 1: 56% yes overall, yes majorities in 5 of 6 states", "Passes", "Both tests are met: a majority overall and a majority in at least four states."]
    - ["Proposal 2: 51% yes overall, yes majorities in 3 of 6 states", "Fails", "A majority overall, but only three states. It needed at least four."]
    - ["Proposal 3: 48% yes overall, yes majorities in 4 of 6 states", "Fails", "Four states, but not a majority overall."]
    - ["Proposal 4: 53% yes overall, yes majorities in 4 of 6 states", "Passes", "Both tests are met."]
```

## Wider: other countries' rulebooks

```step
stage: make
tier: wider
insight: "Not every country puts its rules in one document, and not every written constitution can be changed the same way."
check: { type: reflect, text: "I looked up how one other country's rules for its government are set out (one document, or not), and said one difference from Australia's Constitution to a partner." }
```

Typical and wider steps are extras on the same idea. You do not need them to finish the lesson.

```teacher
summary: "Students see through a made-up club that a constitution sets up
  decision-makers, limits them, and says how the rules themselves change. They
  then meet Australia's Constitution as the same idea at national size: it came
  into effect on 1 January 1901, sets up Parliament, the Governor-General and
  the High Court, limits what Parliament can make laws about, and can be changed
  only by the voters at a referendum. This is the first of two hinge lessons: if
  students do not see the Constitution as the source of the institutions'
  authority, those institutions will look like arbitrary arrangements in the
  lessons that follow."
time: 40
timing: Predict and Try 8 min · Worked example 12 min · Vary 8 min · Practise 6
  min · Make 6 min. Typical and wider steps are extras and not counted in this.
goals:
  - I can say what Australia's Constitution is and when it came into effect.
  - I can name three bodies it sets up and say what each one does.
  - I can explain why Parliament cannot change the Constitution on its own.
struggle: "Students often treat the Constitution as 'just a big law' that
  Parliament can change whenever it likes. The club is there to fix that: ask
  'Could the committee change its own spending limit alone?' and let them work
  out why not before you say it. Resist settling it for them: the argument is
  the learning."
before: >
  This is a hinge lesson. Every later lesson in this course (representative
  government, the separation of powers, federation) assumes students see the
  Constitution as the source of the institutions and their limits. If this
  lesson goes thinly, those institutions will look like arbitrary arrangements.
  Spend the time here.


  Where the club comparison breaks down (say so before students stretch it too
  far): a club's rules can usually be changed by a simple vote of the members,
  while Australia's Constitution needs a double majority at a referendum; and
  the High Court can rule that a law is outside the Constitution, which a club
  has nothing like.


  Everything in the club is made up (Maple Street Chess Club, Nib, Mei, Sam).
  The Constitution, Parliament, the Governor-General and the High Court are real
  and described as they are set out in the Constitution. The referendum results
  in the wider step are made up. No current office holders, parties or live
  policy debates are used.


  Not covered here, on purpose: how Parliament works day to day (next lesson),
  the 1975 dismissal of a Prime Minister, and real referendums such as 1967. If
  you want 1975 as a case of the Governor-General's role, bring it in yourself
  once students have lesson 2. The 1967 referendum belongs with citizenship
  (Freedoms and taking part).


  The Constitution as it was written in 1901 did not treat Aboriginal and Torres
  Strait Islander peoples as citizens in the way it treated other Australians.
  This course writes no explanation of that for students. It is taken up in
  Freedoms and taking part (AC9HC7K02 waypoint 4). If your class raises it,
  start from the school's own resources and local, community-approved material.
running:
  - "Predict: ask for votes before the answer. 'Committee changes the rule then
    spends' is a good one to argue about: why would that make the rule
    pointless?"
  - "Try: stop at 'how the rules themselves can be changed'. This is the item
    the real Constitution answers with a referendum."
  - "Worked example: let Nib's mistake sit before explaining it. Ask students to
    go back to the club."
  - "Vary: ask them to give the reason, not only the answer."
  - "Make: read one or two out if students are happy to, without names."
stuck:
  - see: A student says Parliament can change the Constitution because it makes the
      laws.
    ask: Could the club committee change its own spending limit alone? What would
      the limit be worth then?
    fix: A rule that the rule-makers could change alone would not limit them.
      Parliament can propose a change; the voters decide.
  - see: A student says the Constitution is a list of all of Australia's laws.
    ask: Who makes the laws about passports and tax?
    fix: Parliament does, by passing ordinary laws, inside the limits the
      Constitution sets. The Constitution sets up the system.
  - see: A student thinks the Prime Minister is in the Constitution.
    ask: Look at the three bodies. Is the Prime Minister one of them?
    fix: The Prime Minister is not named in the Constitution. Lesson 2 takes this
      up.
stretch: Why might the people who wrote the Constitution have made it hard to
  change? What would be the risk of making it very easy? This is the same idea
  at greater width. It does not go on to the next lesson.
support: "A card with the three parts of a constitution: sets up the
  decision-makers, limits them, says how the rules change. Students find each
  one in the club and then in Australia."
leads: >
  Next in How Australia is governed: representative and responsible government,
  where the Constitution's institutions meet the voters.


  First Nations content: the elaborations for AC9HC7K01 are about the system of
  government, not First Nations content, so this lesson has no First Nations
  step. See the note above on the Constitution and citizenship.


  ACARA elaborations for AC9HC7K01 (examples, not a checklist): describing
  Australia's system of responsible and representative government set out in the
  Australian Constitution, with a focus on the roles of the Governor-General,
  the Senate and the House of Representatives, the Prime Minister and Cabinet,
  the Opposition and the members of parliament; explaining the origins of the
  Australian system of government by acknowledging the aspects of the
  Westminster and Washington systems in the overall model of Australia's
  Federation; exploring key democratic concepts, including popular sovereignty,
  representation, accountability and a partial separation of powers;
  investigating Australia as a federation with a division of powers and
  responsibilities between Commonwealth and state/territory governments.
exit:
  q: Why can't Parliament change the Constitution on its own?
  a: The Constitution limits Parliament. If Parliament could change it alone, it
    would not limit anything. Only the voters, at a referendum, can approve a
    change.
explain: >
  The **Constitution** is Australia's rulebook for the national government. It
  came into effect on 1 January 1901.


  It sets up Parliament, the Governor-General and the High Court, and it limits
  what Parliament can make laws about. Parliament cannot change it alone: the
  voters decide, at a referendum.
sources:
  - title: The Constitution (Parliamentary Education Office)
    url: https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/the-australian-constitution/the-constitution
    checked: 2026-10-30
  - title: The Australian Constitution (Parliamentary Education Office)
    url: https://peo.gov.au/assets/Public/Australian_Constitution.pdf
    checked: 2026-10-30
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Maple Street Chess Club's committee wants to spend $500, but the rule says
      $200 without asking members. Tom says 'the committee runs the club, so it
      can change the rule.' Ana says 'then the rule means nothing.' Who is
      right, and what would change your mind?
    prompts:
      - What is the rule for, if the committee can change it alone?
      - Who should have the final say on changing it, and why?
    notes: "Steer students to the purpose of the rule: to limit the committee. Do
      not name Parliament yet. The next step does that."
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: activity
      title: Vote with your feet
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Put the four options on the wall, one per corner. Read out the chess
        club situation and have students stand at the corner they pick. Ask
        someone in each corner for a reason.
      notes: The corner for 'changes the rule then spends' usually has the best talk.
        Ask what the rule would be worth.
    - at: make
      kind: discussion
      title: What would go wrong?
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Ask pairs: if Parliament could change the Constitution by voting, what
        could go wrong? Collect a few ideas and ask what they have in common.
      notes: The common thread is that rules which the rule-makers can change alone do
        not limit them.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Who can change it?
      type: question
      q: Who can approve a change to Australia's Constitution?
      options:
        - The voters, at a referendum
        - Parliament, by voting
        - The Governor-General
        - The High Court
      answer: 0
      explain: Parliament can propose a change, but the voters decide.
```
